description: Tricep dips are a bodyweight pushing exercise that isolates the triceps brachii, with secondary involvement of the anterior deltoids and lower pectorals. Performed on parallel bars or a bench, the movement demands shoulder stability and controlled elbow flexion. Depth and control are the two most important factors — going too deep or too shallow both undermine the exercise's effectiveness and safety.
cues: Set up with straight arms and locked elbows to start — this is your top position
Keep your torso upright and slightly leaning forward — do not go fully vertical
Lower yourself until your elbows reach exactly 90 degrees — no deeper
Think about driving your palms down into the surface to push yourself up
Keep your elbows pointing straight behind you — not flaring out to the sides
Controlled descent — do not drop. Imagine you are lowering onto a bed of nails
rules: Keep elbows pointing backward throughout the movement
Lower until elbows reach approximately 90 degrees
Keep shoulders stable — do not shrug toward ears
Stay close to the bench or parallel bars — do not drift forward
Push through palms to return to the top position
Control the movement — no dropping, no bouncing
constraints: Do not flare elbows out to the sides
Do not shrug shoulders up toward ears
Do not drift forward away from the bench or bars
Avoid going too shallow — elbows must be at least 90 degrees
Avoid using momentum or bouncing at the bottom
Do not lock elbows aggressively at the top

elbow_flare.cause: Tight pectorals drawing elbows outward, or incorrect hand placement.
elbow_flare.consequence: Shifts load from the triceps onto the front deltoid and places the shoulder in a vulnerable impingement position.
elbow_flare.fix: Consciously squeeze elbows toward each other throughout the movement. Imagine there is a ball between your arms you are gripping.

shoulder_shrugging.cause: Weak shoulder depressors or the body trying to cheat by using upper traps to initiate the push.
shoulder_shrugging.consequence: Neck and upper trap strain. Also reduces tricep involvement because the movement becomes a shoulder elevation.
shoulder_shrugging.fix: Before you dip, actively pull your shoulders down away from your ears. Hold them there throughout every rep.

forward_drift.cause: Drifting away from the bench changes the exercise into more of a chest dip and unloads the triceps.
forward_drift.consequence: The chest and anterior delt take over — you are no longer doing a tricep dip effectively.
forward_drift.fix: Keep your back brushing the bench or bar throughout. Think: straight down, straight up.

shallow_depth.cause: Stopping before elbows reach 90 degrees, often due to fatigue or to make reps easier.
shallow_depth.consequence: The tricep is only trained in its shortened position — the most important stretch point never loads the muscle properly.
shallow_depth.fix: Aim for at least 90 degrees at the elbow. If you cannot reach it with good form, build strength with negatives.

using_momentum.cause: Bouncing at the bottom to generate upward force instead of using tricep strength.
using_momentum.consequence: Puts sudden high stress on the elbow joint at an already vulnerable flexed position.
using_momentum.fix: Pause for one second at the bottom. Then drive up smoothly and with control.

too_deep.cause: Elbow bending past 90 degrees puts significant strain on the anterior shoulder capsule.
too_deep.consequence: Risk of shoulder impingement and anterior capsule stress — a very common dip injury.
too_deep.fix: Stop the descent when your elbows form a right angle. Do not chase extra depth — it provides no additional benefit.

tilt.note: Forward lean angle — small forward tilt is acceptable in dips

acceleration.note: Spike means you are dropping — stay controlled
